Leasehold redevelopment site in Jalan Merbok for sale; potential for senior living use
article:
A plot of land at Jalan Merbok, off Jalan Jurong Kechil, has been launched for sale via an expression of interest (EOI) exercise.

No guide price has been indicated for the site, according to exclusive marketing agent Knight Frank Singapore. Interested parties are invited to submit an offer together with a proposed concept for the site.

The 94,907 sq ft site is zoned for “Educational Institution” use under the URA Master Plan 2025, and will come with a fresh 103-year leasehold tenure.

Preferred uses include senior living and care facilities such as assisted living, a nursing home, day care centre or training centre for health and medical care, subject to the relevant planning and regulatory approvals, adds the firm.

The site is next to an existing spirituality centre run by non-profit Canossa Mission Singapore, the local mission arm of the Canossian Sisters, at 100 Jalan Merbok.

A project on the redevelopment site could thus potentially serve as a care and community campus that is complementary to the spirituality centre, Knight Frank suggested.

“This co-location provides the potential for a differentiated environment centred on care, wellbeing, reflection and community engagement, while the respective uses remain independently operated,” the marketing agent added.

Located in the Toh Tuck landed housing area, near Bukit Batok, Beauty World and Upper Bukit Timah, the site sits within a mature residential catchment of both private and public housing.

“As senior residents’ care needs evolve, it is ideal for them to transit between different levels of support while remaining within the subject site, helping to reduce disruption for both residents and their families,” said Melvin Chay, interim head of capital markets at Knight Frank Singapore.

Mary Sai, executive director of capital markets at Knight Frank Singapore, expects demand for senior living and care assets to increase as Singapore’s population ages, with those aged 65 and above currently making up 21.6% of the population.

“The subject site offers investors and operators the opportunity to create a differentiated senior-living proposition centred on improved care, wellbeing and quality of life,” said Sai.

The EOI exercise will close on Nov 6 at 3pm.

title: Six units at Nouvel 18, New Futura linked to money laundering case head to auction
article:
Four units at freehold development Nouvel 18 in District 10 and a four-bedder at New Futura along Leonie Hill Road will be going under the hammer at SRI’s upcoming auction on Oct 28.

The properties are among the assets forfeited in Singapore’s $3 billion money laundering case.

In late August, Deloitte Singapore said more than 1,000 luxury items, including jewellery, watches and handbags, as well as 80 real estate properties forfeited in Singapore’s $3 billion money laundering case, would be auctioned in phases between September 2026 and mid-2027.

Deloitte was appointed by the Singapore police last year to manage and realise the non-cash assets seized in connection to the money laundering case.

The latest properties come on the back of 10 apartments at Martin Modern and Wallich Residences that were put on the block in September. Four apartments — two from each development — were successfully sold at auction , with prices ranging from $2.08 million to $6.6 million.

Five luxury apartments at Nouvel 18 up for auction

The five residences at Nouvel 18 are priced from $2,939 psf to $3,558 psf. They comprise four unit types — two- and three-bedroom + study units, and three- and five-bedders — ranging from 1,335 to 6,125 sq ft.

Located in the exclusive Ardmore Park area, Nouvel 18 houses 156 units across two 36-storey residential blocks. It was completed in 2014 and includes facilities such as a swimming pool, BBQ clubhouse, gym, tennis court, and concierge service for its residents.

The freehold luxury development along Anderson Road is about a five-minute drive away from retail and lifestyle amenities at the Orchard Road shopping belt.

“With five units being offered at auction, buyers have multiple opportunities to secure a freehold residence within a development that offers privacy, comprehensive facilities and close proximity to Orchard Road,” said Mok Sze Sze, managing partner of SRI Auction.

Four-bedder at New Futura on the block

In District 9, the four-bedroom unit at New Futura spans 2,691 sq ft with a guide price of $9.8 million, or $3,642 psf.

Mok added that the home’s “generous layout” offers substantial living space for families seeking a home in Singapore’s established prime residential districts.

New Futura is a 124-unit freehold condominium completed in 2017. It is within a 10-minute walk of Somerset MRT Station, with a range of lifestyle, dining and retail amenities nearby at Great World and along Orchard Road at Cineleisure, 111 Somerset , and Ngee Ann City .

The auction for the units at Nouvel 18 and New Futura will take place at 2.30 pm on Oct 28 at SRI’s Great World office.

title: Yangzijiang Has a US$22.4 Billion Order Book: Is the Stock Still a Buy?
article:
Yangzijiang Shipbuilding (Holdings) Ltd.
(SGX: BS6), or YZJ, has an order backlog that stands at a hefty US$22.4 billion.
However, having a hefty order book doesn’t guarantee much if profits start to shrink or the valuation gets too rich.
So, is YZJ still a bargain, or has the market already priced in its best days?
We look at the headline numbers and pay attention to what kinds of vessels it is building.
We’ll also analyse its profit margins, and whether cash flow is actually coming in, and how current contract prices stack up.

Is the Order Book Translating Into Higher Earnings and Cash Flow?
YZJ is not just accumulating orders for headline scale.
In fact, it is actively turning its backlog into expanding profits.
In the first half of 2026 (1H2026), revenue rose 36.2% year on year (YoY) to RMB 17.5 billion.
Shipbuilding gross margin widened to 37.1% from 35.2% a year ago, while profit attributable to shareholders climbed 28.4% to RMB 5.4 billion.
The main driver here is execution on higher-value contracts.
YZJ is now building ships it won at better prices, like ultra-large containerships and very large ethane carriers.
Its new Hongyuan yard also began contributing, chipping in RMB 545 million in second-quarter revenue.
Is cash keeping pace with profit? Not quite yet.
Free cash flow
rose 82% to RMB 675.4 million, which is roughly an eighth of attributable profit.
Since cash flow ultimately underpins distributions, this conversion gap is worth watching as build cycles progress.
Adding to its US$22.4 billion backlog, YZJ continues to win new orders.
By July, it had secured US$1.96 billion in new orders.
That puts the group 43.6% of the way towards its full-year target of US$4.5 billion.

Which Singapore Marine Stock Is a Better Buy: Yangzijiang or Seatrium?
Can YZJ Sustain Its Dividend Growth?
The group pays
dividends
annually, with its FY2025 final dividend of S$0.20 per share paid out in May 2026.
That represented a striking 67% jump over the S$0.12 paid for FY2024.
On an earnings basis, the distribution is easily covered.
A 50% payout ratio leaves half of its record RMB 8.64 billion annual net profit retained in the business, providing ample internal funding for day-to-day operations.
While half-year free cash flow trails net profit due to heavy working capital needs and ongoing yard construction, payout stability is safeguarded by liquidity.
The group maintains an RMB 12.5 billion net cash cushion on its balance sheet.
This financial buffer gives management ample breathing room to fund its LNG terminal and yard expansion projects while rewarding shareholders.
Crucially, higher payouts reflect structural profit expansion rather than one-off distributions, keeping YZJ’s dividend trajectory on firm footing.
What Could Derail the Growth Story?
A US$22.4 billion backlog provides extraordinary top-line visibility, but it is far from risk-free revenue.
First, rising production costs can easily squeeze gross margins.
Shipbuilding contracts operate on fixed pricing, so any sudden spikes in steel plate prices, rising local labour costs, or equipment supply-chain bottlenecks hit profitability directly.
Currency movements are another risk.
Most contracts are priced in USD, while yard costs are paid in RMB, and YZJ does not hedge its currency exposure.
A sharp fall in the USD against the RMB could reduce reported earnings, although management said the recent gradual strengthening of the RMB has had only a limited effect.
Competition, especially from other Chinese and South Korean shipbuilders, could also weigh on YZJ’s future order numbers.
To win contracts, the company could face pressure to accept lower prices on new deals.
If global shipping demand takes a dive from
geopolitical issues
, filling its order books for deliveries past 2029 could also get harder.
Related articles:
Top SGX Stocks Q3 2026: Only 4 Blue Chips Beat the STI
Yangzijiang vs ST Engineering: Which Singapore Growth Stock Would I Buy?
Is the Stock Still Attractively Valued?
Trading at S$5.08 as of 5 October 2026, YZJ shares are valued at around 10.8 times the past 12 months’ earnings.
Based on next year’s expected earnings, however, the stock’s forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio falls to 9.2x, suggesting the market is pricing in steady execution rather than excessive speculative growth.
To put this pricing into perspective, YZJ historically traded at a median trailing P/E of roughly 6.2x during previous industry cycles.
That premium reflects a changed business.
Over the past three years, the group has shifted its vessel mix away from basic dry bulk carriers towards high-margin, dual-fuel LNG containerships and clean-energy gas carriers.
Meanwhile, its 3.2x price-to-book (P/B) ratio remains well supported by a strong 23.6% five-year average return on equity (ROE), and a 3.9% trailing dividend yield provides a steady cash return while investors wait.
Looking ahead, investors should track progress towards the group’s US$4.5 billion full-year order target.
The real test is whether it keeps winning new contracts for tankers and gas carriers, locking in delivery slots for 2029 and 2030 at premium prices.
Also, keep an eye on shipbuilding gross margins, how well progress payments turn into free cash flow, and what’s happening with the USD-RMB exchange rate.
Get Smart: A Big Order Book Is Only the Starting Point
A US$22.4 billion backlog is impressive and gives a clear picture of future revenue, but big contracts don’t automatically guarantee strong, lasting returns.
What actually drives value is how well YZJ turns those orders into higher profit margins, steady free cash flow, and consistent dividends for shareholders.
So, the main thing investors need to figure out isn’t just whether the company has a full pipeline of deals.
Rather, it’s about how skilfully YZJ can turn those deals into real profit.
More importantly, investors need to know whether its current share price still offers real potential for growth over time.

title: Get Smart: Interest Rates Hiked, Are S-REITs Doomed to Mediocrity?
article:
It finally happened.
The US Federal Reserve
raised interest rates
by 0.25% on 16 September 2026.
More increases have been signalled.
S-REITs, which have spent six difficult years adjusting to
higher borrowing costs
, now face the question again: can they cope with another round of rate hikes?
Many will remember the damage interest rates inflicted on S-REITs two years ago.
It begs the question: are S-REITs doomed to mediocrity again?
The answer depends less on where rates end up and more on how quickly they get there.
Did REITs cope with the last round of gradual hikes?
Between 2015 and 2018, the Fed raised rates in 0.25% increments over a three-to-four-year period.
The increases were predictable and spaced out.
Many S-REITs grew their distribution per unit (DPU) throughout that entire cycle.
For instance,
Mapletree Logistics Trust
(SGX: M44U), or MLT, raised its DPU from S$0.075 in its financial year ended 31 March 2015 (FY15) to S$0.07941 in FY19.
And MLT isn’t the only one.
The same can be said of
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U) and
Parkway Life REIT
(SGX: C2PU).
Tellingly, all three are from different industries.
There is a reason why these REITs were able to do so, in our eyes.
REITs operate under long-term contracts on both sides of their balance sheet.
Their tenants sign multi-year leases.
Their lenders extend loans with fixed maturity dates.
A REIT cannot walk into its bank tomorrow and refinance every loan, nor can it approach its tenants mid-lease and demand higher rents.
It is bound by what it has already signed.
Gradual rate hikes give REITs time to work within these constraints.
As leases expire, they renew at higher rents that reflect the new rate environment.
As loans mature, they refinance at whatever rate the market offers.
The income side and the cost side adjust in parallel, and the REIT absorbs the change without squeezing its distributions.
Why did the 2022-2023 cycle catch REITs off guard?
In contrast, the
rate-hike cycle
that began in 2022 was not gradual.
It was the steepest increase in roughly 35 years.
Between March 2022 and July 2023, the US federal funds rate climbed from near zero to 5.5% in under two years.
That steep increase left almost no room for adjustment.
REITs were locked into existing leases that reflected a near-zero rate world.
Their floating-rate loans repriced immediately at far higher costs, while their rental income stayed flat until leases came up for renewal.
The mismatch between fast-rising costs and slow-moving revenue squeezed DPUs across the sector.
The damage showed up in earnings over 2024 and 2025, when higher borrowing costs started to bite into distributable income.
Very few S-REITs came through this period with their DPU intact.
A handful managed to grow distributions every single year from 2020 through to today — a stretch that included a pandemic, tariff disruptions, and the sharpest rate spike in a generation.
They were the exception, not the norm.
Where do rates sit today?
The current US federal funds rate sits at around 4%.
That is higher in the pre-2022 world, but it remains 1.5 percentage points below the 2023–2024 peak of 5.5%.
This gap matters for REITs in a specific way.
Any loan taken out or refinanced near the 2023–2024 peak can now be renewed at a lower rate, even after the latest increase.
S-REITs that locked in borrowing at those elevated levels would actually see their interest costs fall when they next refinance, as long as rates stay below 5.5%.
The risk is not today’s rate level.
Instead, the risk is whether the Fed’s signalled increases come gradually or steeply.
A measured path from 4% to 5%, spread over two years with predictable 0.25% steps, gives REITs the same adjustment window that made 2015–2018 manageable.
A rapid march back towards 5.5% in under a year would recreate the same mismatch that hurt the sector in 2022 and 2023.
Get Smart: It’s about pacing
When rates rise, the reaction is to ask whether your REIT can survive higher borrowing costs.
That question skips the refinancing cycle that is more important.
REITs do not fail because rates are high.
They get squeezed when rates rise faster than their leases and loans can adjust.
The next time the Fed signals a hike, check your REIT’s weighted average debt maturity and lease expiry profile.
A REIT with well-staggered maturities on both sides of its balance sheet may be able to digest gradual increases without cutting its DPU.

title: Bitcoin falls as US$600 mil in risky crypto bets wiped out
article:
(Oct 7): Cryptocurrencies fell on Wednesday as a wave of forced selling swept across digital-asset venues, with broader market jitters further weighing on risk appetite.

Bitcoin, the largest token, fell as much as 2.5% to US$83,470 while ether slumped 4.9% to US$2,567. Other smaller digital assets also fell, with XRP and Solana down 4.2% and 3.4% respectively.

The retreat accelerated as leveraged bets were unwound, with around US$609 million in crypto positions liquidated over the last 24 hours, according to Coinglass data.

“The dip in crypto prices serves as a leverage flush instead of a downward trend, stemming from crowded bets on higher prices being forced out, with most of the liquidations coming from long positions,” said Dan Khus, chief analyst at LVRG Research.

The crypto losses reflected a broader cooling in appetite for risk as renewed Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz tempered hopes that shipping through the key waterway may return to pre-war levels, pushing Brent crude above US$101 a barrel.

See also: Bitcoin bulls descend on Singapore in search of next bet

US stocks' futures edged lower after the S&P 500 closed at an all-time high in the prior session. Europe’s Stoxx 600 snapped three straight days of gains while a recovery in bonds also lost steam, with the 10-year Treasury yield climbing above 5.3%.

Traders are watching the release of Federal Reserve meeting minutes later on Wednesday for clues to the outlook for interest rates, said Rachael Lucas, an analyst at BTC Markets. “A hawkish read could lift yields and the US dollar, keeping pressure on risk assets,” Lucas said.

The slump in crypto prices comes after a recovery from bitcoin’s summer lows, although it remains well off its peak of US$126,000 a year ago.

Trading may remain choppy for the rest of the week in the absence of a fresh catalyst, according to Pratik Kala, a portfolio manager at Apollo Crypto. “If we lose US$83,000, it is possible we revisit the US$78,000 region for bitcoin, which should provide some support,” he said.

title: Thailand puts Bangkok on 24-hour flood watch for IMF meetings
article:
(Oct 7): Thailand is deploying a 24-hour weather and flood-monitoring team for the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group meetings in Bangkok.

The preparations come as more than 15,000 delegates are due in the capital, with thunderstorms, strong winds and brief bursts of heavy rain forecast on Oct 10 and 11. Severe flooding just weeks ago inundated roads, disrupted flights and temporarily shut factories.

Meteorologists will monitor conditions around the clock and issue forecasts district by district, with officials stationed at the meetings throughout the event, Meteorological Department’s forecasting chief Surapong Sarapa said.

title: We have to thank the bond markets for telling the truth: Tharman
article:
In recent times, it is not politicians, but bond vigilantes, who hold the most power over the global economy. In 2022, then-newly minted UK Prime Minister Liz Truss presided over a meltdown in the UK government bond market after her government announced sweeping tax cuts without any corresponding spending adjustments.

Bond vigilantes punished Truss’ largesse severely by voting with their feet and selling off their UK government bonds. Yields spiked and the Bank of England was forced to buy back bonds to stabilise the market. Truss’ premiership was cut short unceremoniously, ending in just 45 days.

“I can’t help thinking that we have to thank the bond markets,” says President Tharman Shanmugaratnam during a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Kristalina Georgieva and National University of Singapore economics professor Danny Quah at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy on Oct 7.

The fireside chat place took place after Georgieva had delivered her curtain raiser speech for the IMF’s upcoming annual meetings, slated to be held in Bangkok, Thailand next week.

“The bond markets are a blessing in disguise. We have learnt that, partly because of polarised and fragmented electorates, leaders in the affected countries are not going to volunteer the truth until they have no choice. They are not going to force painful choices on the electorate until they have no choice. The bond markets are literally the only discipline we have now,” Tharman says.

“They are forcing the issue, and they are telling everyone that, ‘Well, if you don’t act on this step, it’s going to go to the next step.’ In other words, not only do you not have a free lunch, but lunch gets more and more expensive.”

See also: Singapore sees Southeast Asia thriving amid ‘breakdown’ of world order

This appears to be what is happening right now with the US Treasury market after US national debt levels rose to US$40 trillion, or 6% of its GDP, in August. On Oct 5, 10- and 30-year Treasury yields rose to 5.34% and 5.7% respectively, the highest it has been in 24 years.

Earlier, in September, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tried to lower bond yields by announcing a plan to buy up to US$6 billion worth of long-dated Treasuries. The buyback, however, did little to assuage bond investors, who responded by selling off their Treasuries, sending yields even higher.

“So, thank the bond markets. It’s not yet a meltdown. It’s not a revolt. You don’t have what we had in 2022 in the UK, not yet, but it could happen. It’s a warning, a very clear warning and governments need to now sit back and realise these aren’t market disorders,” Tharman says.

See also: Central banks should have a ‘prudently hawkish bias’: IMF chief

“These are actually rational signals from a multitude of players in global markets, telling us you’ve reached the limit, and now you have to make hard choices, and that can be an advantage politically.”

Tharman is no stranger to the IMF’s work. Before assuming the presidency in September 2023, he spent 22 years in politics, where he served as Deputy Prime Minister, Finance Minister and Chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) among other roles.

From 2011 to 2014, Tharman chaired the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC). The committee advises and reports to the IMF Board of Governors on the supervision of the global monetary and financial system.

In Tharman’s view, governments around the world are increasingly more willing to impose their will on central banks, viewing them as an extension of fiscal policy through measures such as quantitative easing.

Even though countries are now gradually pulling back on quantitative easing (QE), Tharman reckons that there are two more subtle forms of fiscal dominance lurking subtly in the shadows.

“Governments are now starting from a position of large fiscal deficits and very high debts as a starting point. Their ability to deal with future crises is now much constrained. Their room for manoeuvre is much constrained. If you get another Covid-like situation, or a recession, or some turbulence in the AI cycle and capex gets withdrawn very quickly, governments cannot step in the way they did in Covid because [there is] no fiscal space,” Tharman says.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

“The burden will fall on central banks and it will fall, increasingly with each crisis, on central banks to have to ease monetary policy. Maybe another round of QE. That will lead over time, on average, to lower interest rates than should be the case, more leverage in the system and ultimately less credibility.”

Besides that, governments are going to have to grapple with disorderly market conditions more often. According to Tharman, what happened to Liz Truss in 2022 may have been an extreme case but there is a possibility of similar events happening down the line.

“When you're operating at very high levels of debt, and when the investors purchasing your debt are now no longer just the traditional, stable, patient, sovereign investors, but you've got a very large proportion of your investors who are hedge funds and other leveraged players with much more complex trading strategies, from time to time there's going to be disorder. And again, who steps in to resolve the disorder? It's the central banks, because they do have that responsibility of financial stability,” Tharman says.

As such, countries will need to build up their fiscal buffers if they want to weather the next crisis more effectively. Tharman cites the example of Portugal, a country he says he was most impressed by when he was chair of the IMFC.

“Portugal realised, when it had spreads of about 1,200 basis points, in other words, 12 percentage points higher than German sovereign bonds, that it had no choice,” Tharman says.

“But Portugal, with all the imperfections of the IMF programme at the time, got good advice, and most important [of all], it took ownership. It took national ownership of the problem. There was no more bluffing.”

Portugal was able to lower its fiscal deficit in a socially progressive manner, Tharman adds. The country’s upper and middle class bore the brunt of the adjustments while the pay and pensions of the lower classes were left untouched.

“It wasn't just about cutting expenditures and raising taxes. It is about going for efficiencies,” Tharman says. “So, efficiency, design, fairness. These are very important principles. It's not just a brutal macroeconomic adjustment. It's about [the] redesign of fiscal policy.”

title: Singapore sees Southeast Asia thriving amid ‘breakdown’ of world order
article:
(Oct 7): Singapore’s top diplomat touted what he called “a moment of great potential” for Southeast Asia, as economies expand rapidly on surging technology demand even as much of the world faces growing uncertainties.

Speaking during a conference on Wednesday, Minister for Foreign Affairs Vivian Balakrishnan said semiconductors and artificial intelligence (AI) were major drivers helping the region’s economies outperform expectations. He noted that the city-state expanded 6.1% in the first half of the year, with Taiwan overtaking China to become its biggest trading partner.

“In the midst of a crazy world, in the midst of the breakdown in world order, the breakdown in trade, the disruption to supply chains, we’re having significant growth,” he said. “In fact, to the point where you start having to worry — why is it so high?”

Asia’s powerhouse economies have seized the lion’s share of trade growth in the global AI boom, because they make the chips and other equipment needed for data centres springing up around the globe. The World Bank cites several Asian economies that have outpaced expectations on high-tech exports, with Vietnam expected to grow 7.4% in 2026, Indonesia 5.2% and Malaysia 5.1%.

Singapore’s electronics exports surged 132% in August from a year earlier, and the island nation has upgraded its 2026 economic growth forecast to between 4.5%-5.5%. Vietnam and Malaysia have likewise strengthened their roles in electronics supply chains as firms spread production across more locations.

See also: Central banks should have a ‘prudently hawkish bias’: IMF chief

But the World Bank has also warned that the region’s dependence on AI-related industry could become a weakness if global investment in the technology slows.

Balakrishnan acknowledged the risks posed by the technology itself, saying “loss of control is a real threat”. He also said rogue states and non-state actors could use AI to develop new forms of disruption, including in chemistry, biology and weapons of mass destruction.

Still, with Singapore set to chair the regional bloc known as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations next year, the diplomat said the region should use the momentum to deepen economic integration.

See also: Yellen says Trump ‘appalling’ on US allies, backs retaliation

“This is a moment of great potential and peril,” Balakrishnan said — later adding: “There’s also a lot of money to be made.”

title: Hong Kong and Singapore pitch rival gold hubs to bullion market
article:
(Oct 7): Officials from Hong Kong and Singapore pitched rival plans to create gold trading hubs in Asia, underscoring fierce competition to secure new business and capitalise on strong demand for the precious metal.

Both financial centres are aiming to plug into established bullion markets by offering new contracts and services, including hosting central bank reserves, and have already secured the participation of local and international banks. Hong Kong launched trial operations of a gold clearing system in July, along with a new price benchmark.

“We are positioning ourselves as a super-connector and also a super value-adder,” Christopher Hui, secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury for Hong Kong, said during a panel discussion at the London Bullion Market Association’s annual meeting in Sorrento, Italy.

The world’s leading industry gathering offered a rare opportunity for representatives of both Asian centers to present their plans at the same forum. Toward the end of the year, Hong Kong will unveil details of offshore-yuan gold futures and allow banks to settle physical trades in real time and in multiple currencies, Hui said.

Singapore’s ambitions are similar. “We are trying to connect different liquidity pools,” Lim Cheng Khai, executive director of the financial markets development department at the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said during the panel session, citing over-the-counter trading in London, the futures market in New York and producers in Asia.

See also: Gold holds gain as lower oil and Fed hike temper inflation fears

Both centres are also courting central banks, whose gold reserves can provide crucial liquidity through lending to commercial financial institutions. Singapore is expanding its storage capacity to become a custodian of bullion held by foreign central banks, while the People’s Bank of China has built up its reserves in Hong Kong in recent months.

Both Hong Kong and Singapore are tapping into a wider move toward diversification, which has already seen some central banks repatriate gold in recent years, challenging the status of historic hubs such as London and New York. Even a small share of the 39,000 tonnes held by central banks globally would bolster either centre’s influence.

“What we are trying to do is not totally new,” Hui, the Hong Kong official, said on the sidelines of the conference. “Rather, we are really riding on this trend of the need to diversify.”

See also: Singapore’s gold hub plan gets lift with DBS vault expansion

Some participants at the LBMA event said there was room for both centres potentially to thrive, given the deep liquidity of the global market. Perhaps the biggest challenge, however, may lie in persuading market participants of the need to switch their business away from more established centers.

“If you talk to anyone, anywhere on the planet, what do you benchmark the price against? It’s the LBMA fix,” Gregory Frith, senior precious metals trader at Centalion, said during a separate panel session. “How do you evolve from that? You have to try and get ahead of the curve.”

Hong Kong’s project has a strong political angle, with the city — already the world’s biggest market for offshore yuan — aiming to leverage gold to drive greater usage of the Chinese currency. It also has the advantage of potential collaboration with China-friendly gold-producing countries, such as Uzbekistan.

Proximity to China, however, might also be viewed as a risk. Centalion’s Frith said that — while he likes Hong Kong contracts — some traders might be more comfortable doing business in Singapore. “For companies and big traders, it all comes down to contracts — where do I feel the most comfortable?” he said.

title: Central banks should have a ‘prudently hawkish bias’: IMF chief
article:
International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Kristalina Georgieva is no stranger to the dangers of inflation. In the mid-1990s, the Bulgarian national watched her country go through a period of hyperinflation.

Inflation soared to 8,300%, wiping out the savings of almost all Bulgarians, including Georgieva’s own mother. Fortunately, Bulgaria’s government took tough but necessary policy actions to remedy the situation. Fast forward to today and Bulgaria’s income per capita has gone up eight times and it became a member of the European Union in 2007.

Witnessing that episode left Georgieva with a heightened awareness of what inflation could do to economies if left unattended. What happened to Bulgaria can happen elsewhere, and right now it is the global economy at large that is grappling with inflation.

“The AI building boom is inflationary. The energy and food shocks are inflationary. Tariffs, defence spending, and high public debt can be inflationary. And memories of the recent high inflation are still fresh,” Georgieva said in her curtain raiser speech for the IMF’s upcoming annual meetings on Oct 7. Georgieva delivered her speech at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy in Singapore, a week before the meetings are slated to commence in Bangkok, Thailand.

Inflation itself has remained persistent. In the US, inflation has exceeded the Federal Reserve’s (Fed) target of 2% for more than five years. But that did not stop the Federal Reserve from cutting interest rates in December 2025 by 25 basis points to between 3.5% and 3.75%.

“We draw comfort from long-term inflation expectations staying anchored, but let us not forget the simple fact that inflation is only anchored until it is not. I learned the hard way from Bulgaria’s hyperinflation, this lesson,” Georgieva says.

See also: We have to thank the bond markets for telling the truth: Tharman

“Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries’ monetary policy. It is highly appropriate that the US Federal Reserve, the ECB (European Central Bank), and the Bank of Japan have all raised rates and spoken firmly, with future policy rate paths repricing accordingly.”

With an end to the Iran war nowhere in sight, policymakers have begun to accept that higher energy prices are here to stay. Even the newly minted Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who had chosen to hold rates steady after taking office in May, had to do an about-face. The Federal Open Market Committee announced on Sept 16 that it had voted unanimously to hike rates by 25 basis points to 3.75% and 4%. Market watchers and analysts are now forecasting at least one more rate hike by the end of this year.

See also: Singapore sees Southeast Asia thriving amid ‘breakdown’ of world order

Asia’s economy has grown by leaps and bounds over the past few decades. According to the IMF’s data, Asia Pacific’s share of global GDP is now at 43% today, up from 25% in 1991.

Georgieva, however, warns in her speech that it could be much harder to sustain global economic growth in the coming years. This is because of three major crosscurrents that are disrupting the world today: the rise of AI, high energy prices and soaring public debt levels.

“To put it simply, the global economy is being pulled in two opposite directions: a negative energy supply shock on the energy side and a positive demand shock from AI,” she says. “The combined impact of these two forces is highly uneven across the world.”

Georgieva expects global investment-to-GDP in AI to surpass the amounts that went into earlier industrial booms, such as the construction of the railroad, electricity grid or telecommunication network. In fact, AI hardware and related products already account for more than 10% of the world’s goods trade and are still rising, she adds.

That said, AI consumes a lot of energy and will add pressure to the present energy shock caused by the war in Iran. Prices of Brent crude continue to trade at around US$100 ($128) per barrel and a structural shortfall in refining capacity are sending prices of diesel and other refined products to record highs, Georgieva says.

“To quote from Game of Thrones, winter is coming. Price pressures may build further as countries replenish reserves and demand rises with the approach of the Northern hemisphere cold season. Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, high energy prices would likely persist for some time. Brent futures, for example, now predict high oil prices through 2027.”

Higher energy prices also have knock on effects, pushing up inflation, interest rates and benchmark yields. This will add even more pressure to the fiscal crunch that advanced economies like the US and Japan are already grappling with. Global public debt is on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP and is nearing levels not seen since after World War II, Georgieva says.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

While some policymakers might be counting on AI to help spur growth, Georgieva cautions against such complacency. AI's capital-intensive nature has led Big Tech companies to turn to debt and equity markets to fund their investments. Bond issuances by hyperscalers will thus be competing against sovereign bond issuances for capital.

“Policymakers had a relatively easy ride over the last 17 years as for all that time interest rates were stuck below GDP growth rates,” Georgieva says. “Now, it is no more the case.”

To best address this, Georgieva urges heavily indebted, advanced countries to lower their reliance on monetary policy. Instead, such countries need to focus on fiscal consolidation and pursue broader structural reforms to revive their economies. This applies to emerging markets as well, which should be trying to expand their fiscal space and foreign exchange buffers.

“Fiscal consolidation will be a heavy lift,” Georgieva says. “After a succession of shocks where, each time, fiscal policy has had to step in to cushion the impact, people have grown accustomed to state support, and yet some very tough political choices stare us in the face.”

title: Temasek CIO says AI, inflation pose biggest market risks in 2027
article:
(Oct 7): Temasek International’s investment chief highlighted the potential for the artificial intelligence (AI) trade to reverse and inflation pushing up bond rates to a point that may end the runup for equities as top risks facing global markets heading into next year.

“The unwinding of the AI trade is the biggest risk,” said Temasek International chief investment officer Rohit Sipahimalani. “We don’t see that as imminent. But, will you have bumps in 2027, possibly yes.”

Speaking at the Milken Asia Summit 2026 in Singapore on Wednesday, Sipahimalani said the other main issue is “concerns around inflation”.

“Inflation is a risk, together with what is happening in the rates environment, that means there probably is a risk of some breaking point in the equity market at some point,” he said. Together with AI, these are “two key risks I would see for 2027”.

Debate is raging ahead of the upcoming US earnings season that will mark a key test of whether hundreds of billions of dollars of AI-related spending by tech giants is following through to stronger profits. Global bonds have slumped as higher energy prices and fiscal borrowing needs push bets on more central bank rate hikes to rein in inflation.

State-owned Temasek, which had $518 billion as of March 31, this year pledged to more than double its allocation to AI-related investments from 6% to up to 15% by 2031. AI has already been a major driver of the firm’s returns — it owns stakes in some of the sector’s biggest names including OpenAI, Anthropic and Nvidia Corp.

See also: Asian stocks hold near record highs, oil climbs

Sipahimalani on Wednesday said he wants to move more of that AI exposure away from private holdings into publicly traded assets. This will help Temasek remain nimble to respond timely if needed, he said.

“AI is such a fast changing environment, things could change quite easily and you have to be able to pivot,” he said.

The firm has around half its AI exposure in public markets, and “we want to increase that number ideally to 70% to 75% so it gives us more flexibility to pivot with changes in the environment, as against being stuck with a private asset which there’s little you can do when things are changing”, he added.

See also: Asia stocks rise after US tech rally, oil steadies

Temasek’s investments in the Americas have surged in recent years, thanks in large part to AI investments, and made up 26% of its portfolio as of March 31.

Speaking on the same panel at the Milken event, Mubadala chief financial officer Carlos Obeid said the Middle Eastern fund has been trying diligently over the last few years to increase its Asia exposure.

“A few years ago, the share of the portfolio that was allocated or invested in Asia was about 10%, it has increased now to about 13% and we want to do more,” he said. “We’ve been present in China mainly, South Korea, Japan and India. And we want to grow those exposures.”

Granite Asia Capital senior managing partner Jenny Lee on the same panel highlighted how the narrrative has changed for allocators’ investing in China.

“I think China has gone from ‘China is not investable’ to ‘Is China investable’ with a question mark to now the most common question I get — ‘are we missing out?’,” she said.

title: Topix’s biggest ever revamp to cull hundreds of Japan stocks
article:
(Oct 7): Japan Exchange Group Inc unveiled the biggest-ever reshuffle of the Topix on Wednesday, a revamp that shrinks one of Asia’s broadest major equity benchmarks and intensifies pressure on Japanese companies to boost their market appeal.

There were 683 companies earmarked for removal under tougher inclusion rules, according to JPX’s announcement. Those slated for gradual removal include Medley Inc and Ichiyoshi Securities Co. Among the 35 stocks that will be added are McDonald’s Holdings Co Japan and Ferrotec Corp. The changes will begin to take effect on Oct 30.

The changes are the second stage of a multiyear effort by the group, which operates the Tokyo Stock Exchange, to make the Topix more investable. The benchmark has long stood out among major global indexes for its large number of constituents, including hundreds of relatively illiquid small-cap companies.

The overhaul has potentially significant implications for global investors. About ¥166 trillion (RM4.3 trillion) in passive assets track the Topix, according to a September estimate by Daiwa Securities chief quantitative analyst Junichi Hashimoto. Companies that are to be dropped face rules-driven selling by index funds while those pencilled for inclusion can generate steady demand from passive investors and will be on the radar of active managers seeking to beat the index.

The first phase of the revamp that ended in January 2025 reduced the number of members to about 1,700 from roughly 2,200. After the latest overhaul, the tally could fall further to just under 1,000 in two years. Cutting the number of constituents should make it easier for investors to run passive strategies tracking the index while encouraging competition among aspiring companies to secure a place in the benchmark.

See also: Suzuki undercuts BYD as competition for cheap mini EVs heats up

Reducing Topix constituents is “basically positive", said Hiromi Ishihara, head of equity investment at Amundi Japan Ltd. As companies increasingly need to justify their inclusion in the index and “if steady reforms at individual companies add up, the Japanese equity market as a whole could gain a higher valuation,” she said.

Ishihara said there have been several cases in which small-cap companies stepped up shareholder returns in an effort to avoid removal from the Topix, helping to lift their share prices. For investors, she said, there are opportunities in determining “whether actions aimed at staying in the index end up being temporary measures to support the share price or lead to genuine increases in corporate value through stronger corporate governance and other reforms.”

Under the new rules, additions and deletions will be determined using criteria including annual traded-value turnover, a measure of how actively shares change hands and the market capitalisation of shares available to public investors.

Stocks selected for removal will not disappear from the index immediately. Their weightings will be reduced quarterly through July 2028. Companies that meet the requirements when they are reassessed in October 2027 can halt that process. From October 2028, the benchmark will be rebalanced annually.

Investors are expected to remain mindful of the risk that small-cap stocks could be removed from Topix going forward and “the trend toward large-cap stocks will likely strengthen”, said Shota Sando, an analyst at Tokai Tokyo Intelligence Lab.

title: Ray Dalio says we’re nearing point where AI bubble may burst
article:
(Oct 7): Billionaire Ray Dalio warned that artificial intelligence (AI) is a “classic bubble” that is nearing a bursting point thanks to rising interest rates and the need to turn wealth into cash.

Speaking at the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore on Wednesday, Dalio said that a huge amount of debt is being taken out to fund AI. As rates continue to climb, that is a point at which the bubble begins to pop.

“We’re in the part of the cycle that is before that but approaching that,” the Bridgewater founder said. “I think we’re close to that.”

His comments come as technology giants spend hundreds of billions of dollars on AI, increasingly financed with debt, and as market gains concentrate in a handful of stocks. Bond yields around the world have surged to the highest in decades, increasing the cost of funding the enormous investment needed to build AI infrastructure.

Still, equity valuations continue to rise, with optimism over technology earnings propelling the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 indices to record highs this week.

Dalio, who has long warned of an AI bubble, said there were other issues that could trigger its collapse. Those include wealth taxes and other efforts to convert unrealised gains into cash.

See also: Nvidia’s valuations show AI rally isn’t a bubble, DBS says

“Everybody says ‘I’m worth a billion dollars’ but OK, try to spend that,” he added. “In order to spend that you have to sell wealth in order to get money — and so the bubble usually pricks at that.”

title: Copper stable as AI-driven tech stock rally holds near record
article:
(Oct 7): Copper steadied as a rally in tech-related stocks held near record highs, driven by optimism about the artificial intelligence boom.

Contracts on the London Metal Exchange were little changed on Wednesday, reflecting broader caution across other markets. The red metal is set to receive a demand boost from data centres built for the AI industry, the same sector driving this week’s gains in global stocks.

The copper market is still in consolidation mode after surging to a record last month when the threat of US tariffs on refined metal prompted a rush of supplies to America, tightening it elsewhere. Traders are awaiting the reopening of markets in China, the world’s top metal consumer, following a week-long national holiday for the next cues on price direction.

Copper futures were steady at US$14,413 a tonne on the LME at 9.55am Singapore time. Aluminium was 0.4% higher while zinc added 0.1%.

title: US court allows fund to obtain documents in Radiant World case
article:
(Oct 7): A US court has allowed a fund managed by Mariner Investment Group to obtain documents from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the Clearing House Interbank Payments System in its Swiss proceedings against iron ore trader Radiant World, according to an order.

Judge John P Cronan of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York allowed the request made by Mariner Atlantic Multi-Strategy LLC, ordering it to provide copies of the decision to all targets. These include Radiant World, group founder Pinkesh Nahar and director Bhupeshkumar Gejvala, as well as related entity Sapphire Minmetals.

The fund has accused Radiant World of fraud and money laundering, and has asked Swiss prosecutors to open a criminal investigation, conduct searches of company premises and seize bank accounts and other assets.

A Radiant World spokesperson had no immediate comment. Mariner did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside business hours.

Radiant World is facing a spate of civil lawsuits from Singapore to London over allegations from creditors that it provided banks with falsified documents to secure financing, while Singapore Police are also conducting an investigation into the company. The company’s main offices are located in Singapore, Switzerland and Dubai.

See also: Korean investors suffer US$1.7 bil losses from leveraged ETFs

title: Beware of stranded assets when data centre boom ‘finally fizzles out’: Ho Kwon Ping
article:
Southeast Asian countries should be wary of the rapid data centre build-out, lest they become stuck with “the most stranded assets” when the data centre boom “finally fizzles out”, says Ho Kwon Ping, founder and executive chairman of Banyan Group.

Speaking at the opening panel of the Forbes Global CEO Conference on Oct 7, Ho warns that some regional markets may be focused on the “immediacy of data centres in terms of what it can do for the investors”, adding that the new-builds offer “not much employment generation”.

“I think we need to have a little bit more of a sceptical look about the proliferation of data centres across Asia, rather than everybody seeing that this is the latest big thing that we should all jump into,” he says.

Ho believes this proliferation echoes the manufacturing boom in Southeast Asia “30 years ago”, when corporates set up factories in the region to produce goods like disc drives. “It’s the same thing — outsourcing to the developing world the most basic AI work, the basic learning and so on.”

Ho also points to the “economics of data centres”. “Most of the data centres that are being set up around Asia are in fact by large funds, where a lot of people have invested into the private equity companies that are making a lot of money, and they’re only contracted to sell to the AI companies themselves with contracts [that] are relatively easy to break. I’m just waiting to see, when this data centre boom finally fizzles out, which country is going to be left with the most stranded assets.”

Discussions around AI are often conflated with the investment boom in AI-related infrastructure. “There’s actually two completely separate threads,” says Ho. “The best parallel to this is the US railroad boom and bust in the 19th century. [It] led to a lot of extremely positive things, [such as the] opening up of all of the US, [but] it also led to a lot of stranded railways all across the US.”

See also: Singapore-based data centre operator BDx breaks ground for an AI data centre in Java

Ho urges caution around the “current boom”. “It’s going to lead to a physical and investment bust, while the rest of the technology continues to benefit the world. It’s two separate issues we should be talking about.”

Further, Ho believes the “weaponisation of AI” is “most likely the next big danger to the world”. “My cynical view when you talk about regulation is that I don’t think you’re going to get China, the US or any country in the world coming together very nicely to talk about regulating AI until some very, very bad intentional or unintentional accident happens.”

Given the current “arms race” between nations over developing AI, however, “it’s kind of fanciful or delusional” to believe companies will “exercise self-restraint” and prioritise the greater good, says V Shankar, co-founder and CEO of Singapore and Dubai-based alternative investment manager Gateway Partners.

See also: New data centres worth US$68 billion disrupted in US, data show

Speaking on the same panel, Shankar says it remains to be seen if the current build-out of data centres is “similar to the fibre optic subsea [cables], where there was huge overcapacity, or is it [similar to] a cloud build-out, where there has not been overcapacity and has actually turned out pretty well”.

Staying on those examples, PwC global chairman Mohamed Kande says the value of these Internet-enabling infrastructure were not found in their build-out or supply, but in the diffusion and adoption of the Internet by users. “It was the adoption of the internet that made a difference, not the supply of the internet.”

Kande adds: “The same thing is going to happen. The societies and the companies that are going to rise [and] benefit from all of this investment in AI — not only companies but societies — are the ones that are going to diffuse and adopt AI at scale.”

title: Korean investors suffer US$1.7 bil losses from leveraged ETFs
article:
(Oct 7): Retail investors are estimated to have lost 2.3 trillion won (US$1.7 billion) from leveraged exchange-traded products tracking South Korea’s two chipmaking giants in just months, according to a lawmaker’s office, in the first revelation of the magnitude of risks from such bets.

Clients of 10 Korean brokerages incurred the losses from single-stock ETFs and notes tied to Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc between May 27 and Aug 14, according to the office of Choi Eun-seok, a lawmaker from the opposition People Power Party.

Since their launch in May, the single-stock products have intensified volatility in Korea’s AI-centric stock market, where leveraged bets have propelled it into one of the world’s top performers before backfiring. The wild swings caused by the risky products have since prompted regulators to cool the fervor among mom-and-pop investors, resulting in a plunge in trading volume.

The data came from the financial watchdog Financial Supervisory Service, which collated information from brokerages including Mirae Asset Securities Co, Kiwoom Securities Co, Samsung Securities Co and NH Investment & Securities Co, Choi’s office said.

Since July, the authorities took measures including a temporary ban on new listings of the leveraged single-stock prodcuts, as well as a higher minimum cash deposit and training requirements for investors. They marked an about-face after regulators introduced the products in May, partly aimed at deterring local investors from piling into similar ETFs listed overseas.

See also: JPMorgan tops global AI banking index with jobs seen to grow

While the leveraged products seek to amplify gains, they can also inflict outsized pain on investors when the tide turns in a market disproportionately exposed to the cycles of the AI industry, where the two Korean chipmakers sit at the centre of its supply chain.

title: Wildfire haze shuts Malaysian schools and looms over Singapore F1
article:
(Oct 7): Worsening air pollution driven by wildfires in Indonesia prompted Malaysia to temporarily shut schools in one of its most populated states, just as a major Formula One race in neighbouring Singapore approaches.

Some 200 schools, kindergartens and nurseries in Johor state’s Bahu Pahat district, about 140km northwest of Singapore, were ordered to close today due to the haze conditions, local media reported. The air quality index in the Malaysian capital of Kuala Lumpur was also in the “very unhealthy” range as of Wednesday morning, ranking the city as the most polluted globally, according to data from IQAir.

Air quality in three of Singapore’s five regions also ranked as unhealthy on Wednesday, days before the city-states’s annual F1 weekend, government data showed.

A spokesperson for Singapore GP Pte Ltd, which organises the race, said it will work closely with relevant agencies “to assess the situation before making any collective decisions regarding the event” should haze cause visibility, public health or operational issues. An F1 spokesperson said conditions are not at any level of concern.

Swaths of Southeast Asia have been clouded in choking smog in recent weeks as Indonesia battles one of its worst wildfire seasons in years. The uncontrolled blazes stem from the long-running use of slash-and-burn agricultural practices, but fire conditions have been exacerbated by an intensifying El Niño that’s parching the landscape.

Environmental group Greenpeace identified more than 20 palm, pulp and sugar companies, including several with links to Malaysia and Singapore, whose land concessions contained sources of smoke from the fires.

See also: Singapore, Malaysia cloaked in haze before key sports events

The number of hotspots last month was the highest since 2015, when a regional haze emergency caused widespread disruptions and diplomatic tensions, according to the Forestry Ministry’s fire-monitoring platform SiPongi.

Last week, organisers of the Kuala Lumpur Standard Chartered Marathon cancelled a kids’ race on health concerns, while pressing on with other race categories, including the full and half marathon distances. Still, top finishers of the full marathon clocked times that were slower than recent years. The marathon was cancelled in 2015.

title: JPMorgan tops global AI banking index with jobs seen to grow
article:
(Oct 6): JPMorgan Chase & Co held its spot as the world’s most advanced bank in artificial intelligence, widening its lead over rivals in an annual ranking that shows AI deployment across the industry is accelerating at a record pace.

Capital One Financial Corp and Royal Bank of Canada retained their second and third places, according to the Evident AI Index that was published on Tuesday. Commonwealth Bank of Australia stayed in fourth position as the only Asia-Pacific lender in the top 10, while UBS Group AG, at sixth place, is the sole European bank in the top leagues. Meanwhile, DBS Group Holdings Ltd, Southeast Asia’s largest bank, ranked 25th, the index showed.

The Evident AI Index seeks to show how global lenders are turning heavy AI spending into results, at a time when banks are facing pressure to justify record tech budgets and concerns brew over whether AI will cost jobs. Lenders that can’t show the technology generates returns risk seeing their AI programs stall, Evident said.

“Roles are changing, and some are not being backfilled, but the banks at the top of our Index are growing, and growing headcount,” Alexandra Mousavizadeh, Evident’s co-founder and co-chief executive officer, said in a statement. “This could be the start of the largest net job creation we have seen in decades.”

Across the 50 banks assessed, AI capabilities improved almost three times faster over the past year than the average across the previous three years, the fastest pace since the index began in 2023.

The leading banks in AI are using productivity gains to grow their business as well as drive efficiencies, Evident said. An example it cites is Wells Fargo & Co training AI agents on 15 years of loan decisions so the process can be automated, with underwriters making the final call.

See also: Taiwan dethrones Korea atop global markets as AI trade widens

Banks are adding AI talent with a focus on enabling people who use the tool, according to Evident, noting that JPMorgan, Commonwealth Bank of Australia and Royal Bank of Canada are the top hirers.

These so-called AI enablement roles, which accelerate deployment of the tech and redesign workflows, grew 21% over the past year across the 50 banks, the fastest of any AI job category. Data engineering roles fell 3%, while other roles like AI development and AI software implementation grew much slower, the Evident report shows.

The index scores the institutions based on their AI talent, research and patent activity, leadership communications and transparency around AI deployment. For JPMorgan, this is the bank’s fifth straight year at the top.

title: Maersk owner seeks investments in Asia startups with new office
article:
(Oct 7): AP Moller Holding A/S, which controls Danish shipping giant AP Moller-Maersk A/S, is opening a new office in Singapore to invest in growth companies in Asia.

The firm, funded entirely by the billionaire Maersk family with no external investors, will open the office — its first outside of Denmark — this week. It has more than US$50 billion ($64 billion) of net assets.

“Asia is at the forefront of global innovation,” said Chetan Mehta, head of growth investing at the firm, who is going to lead the Asia office. “As many of these world-leading late-stage startups are looking to expand, that gives us an opportunity to provide them the long-term funding.”

The Danish investment company is looking to take minority stakes, typically €20 million (US$22.4 million or $28.7 million) to €80 million, from Series C startups to IPO-stage firms and beyond, Mehta said in an interview.

The startups will mostly be in the applied technology sector, such as AI supply chains, fintech, healthcare and robotics. The firm will be looking at firms across China, India, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, he added.

In Europe, AP Moller Holding is an existing investor in French online healthcare platform Doctolib, Finnish satellite maker Iceye and UK fintech giant Revolut. It led the €80 million equity funding round of UK neo-bank Zopa in 2024, and is the largest shareholder of Danske Bank A/S.

See also: Rhine drops below shipping threshold as freight costs rise

“We are investing our own money without a hard exit deadline nor fund life, so we can be really flexible and support the startups along their growth journey,” Mehta said.

title: Taiwan dethrones Korea atop global markets as AI trade widens
article:
(Oct 7): As equity investors enter the final stretch of a pivotal year that’s propelled South Korea and Taiwan to the forefront of the global AI trade, the latter is emerging as the stronger bet.

The Taiex Index beat the Kospi by about 23 percentage points last quarter, the widest margin since the turn of the century. Earnings upgrades also outpaced those for its Korean peer for the first time since March 2025. About 40% of the fund managers surveyed by Bank of America Corp. last month said they were overweight Taiwan, versus 25% for Korea.

Driving the optimism are Taiwan’s deeper linkages across the AI supply chain and a more upbeat earnings outlook.

“The distinction for us is not simply the amount of AI exposure, but the nature of the earnings supporting it,” said Vikas Pershad, a portfolio manager at M&G Investments in Singapore. “Taiwan offers a broader and deeper opportunity set. Its earnings come from volume and that makes its earnings upgrades broader and stickier. Korea’s earnings, in the near-term, are coming from price.”

Taiwan offers investors exposure across chip design and manufacturing, packaging, networking, and servers, meaning it has more ways to benefit as AI spending broadens. Korea’s market leadership, meanwhile, remains heavily concentrated in chipmakers Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc., leaving it more vulnerable as doubts emerge over how much longer the current memory upcycle can run.

See also: Citi takes top spot in global IPO underwriting through September

The Taiex and Kospi have traded places at the top of the global leaderboard this year, even as the latter has dominated headlines for its more eye-catching moves. Up 72% in 2026, Taiwan’s benchmark is currently the top performer among more than 90 equity indexes tracked by Bloomberg. The Kospi is ranked second, with gains of about 65%.

Taiwan’s lead comes as shares of Samsung and SK Hynix plunged between 19% and 33% in the three months ended September. That followed a six-quarter winning streak as surging memory-chip prices drove blockbuster earnings and fueled rapid profit upgrades from analysts.

Societe Generale SA is “keeping a preference for Taiwan over Korean equities, given the diverging earnings growth trajectories,” strategists including Rajat Agarwal wrote in note. Memory “price appreciation is expected to slow over coming quarters, before normalization in 2028” as Chinese competition rises, while Korea’s July deleveraging has broadened into a wider retreat from the market, they wrote.

The counter view is AI-related demand will exacerbate the ongoing semiconductor supply shortage, keeping prices for high-bandwidth memory chips supported. Peter Lee, a managing director at Citigroup Inc who jointly oversees its global tech and communication research, said last week that investors should start buying shares of firms like Samsung and SK Hynix as the market is underestimating how much HBM chips will be needed in 2027.

In terms of valuations, the Taiex is trading at about 18 times its one-year forward estimated earnings. The Kospi trades at around 5.5 times, reflecting concern that the memory cycle may be approaching a peak, and in part the longstanding “Korea discount” that has kept the market cheap relative to global peers.

Still, when asked which market would benefit the most from the next phase of the AI cycle, 35% of the respondents in the BofA survey chose Taiwan. Just 5% picked Korea.

Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. rose 2.9% in the three months to September, capping a sixth straight quarterly advance.

But Taiex is delivering broader gains than its other tech-heavy peers, reflecting a wider range of investment opportunities. About 10% of the gauge’s stocks have at least doubled this year, compared with 4.1% for the Kospi and 5.7% for Japan’s Nikkei 225.

“The next leg of upside for Taiwan stocks is likely to depend less on broad AI enthusiasm and more on local tech companies that remain exposed to genuine bottlenecks in the AI value chain,” said Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments.

title: Oil advances as vessel attacks challenge rising Hormuz shipments
article:
(Oct 7): Oil gained as traders weighed increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz against a pickup in Iranian attacks against vessels.

Brent rose towards US$102 a barrel after a volatile session on Tuesday, while West Texas Intermediate was above US$90. While shipments through Hormuz have expanded in recent weeks, UK Maritime Trade Operations has reported at least nine attacks in the waterway so far this month. That’s already half of the number across Hormuz and the Persian Gulf combined in September.

Tehran was hitting some ships, but not enough to stop the flow of oil and gas, US Vice-President JD Vance told Reuters in an interview. Meanwhile, Washington remained open to an agreement, and was in talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Vance said.

Crude has rallied sharply this year as the US-Iran war disrupted flows from the Middle East, fanning inflation. Leading industry figures including Shell plc chief executive officer Wael Sawan have warned this week that the world is running out of stopgaps to manage the impact of the conflict, with global stockpiles being drawn down and product prices including diesel still elevated.

“The market is starting to believe that barrels can keep getting through,” said Haris Khurshid, chief investment officer at Karobaar Capital LP. Still, depleted inventories and tight diesel supplies mean “the physical market has a lot less cushion than the headline export numbers suggest”, he said.

Middle East oil flows have recovered to about 80% of pre-conflict volumes, Shell’s Sawan told a forum, while Vitol Group chief executive officer Russell Hardy said about 12 million barrels a day of crude exited the strait over the past seven to 10 days. The waterway links the Persian Gulf to global markets.

See also: Oil holds decline on signs of increased Middle East shipments

Separately, Saudi Arabia said it’s now pumping 5.8 million barrels a day through its cross-country pipeline to the Red Sea. The link had been shut last month following attacks by drones that were launched from Iraq.

Later Wednesday, the International Energy Agency is due to hold discussions on plans for an emergency release of up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude inventories pledged by the Group of Seven, people familiar with the matter said. The talks are expected to provide more clarity on how to proceed.

In the US, crude stockpiles contracted by 2.1 million barrels last week, according to an estimate from the industry-funded American Petroleum Institute seen by Bloomberg. The snapshot also showed a drop in gasoline holdings, while distillates rose. Official data are due later Wednesday.

See also: Global oil supply buffer running ‘scarily thin’, Aramco CEO says
• Brent for December settlement gained 1% to US$101.59 a barrel at 9:33 a.m. in Singapore.

US President Donald Trump said he was weighing a suspension of the federal gas tax, as his administration looks for ways to ease costs ahead of November’s midterm elections. Earlier this week, the US leader relaxed rules on the usage of diesel, allowing truckers to burn fuel normally reserved for tractors.

Traders were also monitoring what may become the first Atlantic hurricane of the year. A tropical depression formed about 630 miles (1,014km) south of the Mississippi River’s mouth, the US National Hurricane Center said Tuesday. It is expected to become Tropical Storm Isaias by Wednesday and reach hurricane strength by Thursday, potentially hitting the US Gulf Coast.

While forecasts put the storm east of major offshore oil and natural gas production south of Louisiana and Texas, there could be disruptions depending on its path and size. Chevron Corp said it was evacuating non-essential staff from Gulf of Mexico platforms, but no changes to output had been made.

title: Asian stocks hold near record highs, oil climbs
article:
(Oct 7): Asian shares held near a record after optimism over the earnings outlook propelled Wall Street benchmarks to fresh all-time highs. Crude oil climbed.

MSCI’s Asia Pacific equities gauge was little changed Wednesday, with the regional benchmark less than 2% from its peak. The All Country World Index — a key barometer of global stocks — is about 0.5% away from its high hit in August.

The moves in Asia followed record closes for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100 Index ahead of the US earnings season next week. Artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks led the advance on Tuesday, with Nvidia Corp’s market value approaching US$6 trillion (RM24.52 trillion). Tech remained in focus after the Financial Times reported SpaceX was looking to raise US$40 billion to buy Nvidia chips.

Elsewhere, Brent rose 0.6% to just above US$101 a barrel as traders weighed increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz against a pickup in Iranian attacks against vessels. Treasuries pared their gains from Tuesday, with the benchmark 10-year yield climbing two basis points to 5.30%.

Global stocks are hovering near record highs as investors bet companies can withstand higher interest rates and higher energy costs due to elevated oil prices. With the economic data calendar light, attention will turn to the upcoming earnings season for signs that hundreds of billions of dollars in AI-related spending by tech giants are translating into stronger profits.

“Recent economic growth data have been strong and S&P 500 earnings revision breadth has remained positive,” Goldman Sachs Group Inc. strategists led by Ben Snider wrote in a note. “We expect most companies will once again surpass consensus earnings estimates this quarter.”

See also: Asia stocks rise after US tech rally, oil steadies

Analysts expect a roughly 25% increase in third-quarter S&P 500 profits from a year earlier, according to data compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence.

In Asia, attention is on the diverging performance of Taiwanese and South Korean stocks. The Taiex Index beat the Kospi by about 23 percentage points last quarter, the widest margin since the turn of the century. Driving the optimism are Taiwan’s deeper linkages across the AI supply chain and a more upbeat earnings outlook.

“Korea’s more muted response partly reflects growing caution about the financing behind the AI boom,” said Jung In Yun, chief executive officer at Fibonacci Asset Management Global. “Elevated long-term bond yields are weighing on technology valuations, and increased corporate debt issuance to fund AI capital expenditure may be adding to that pressure.”

See also: It’s my party and I’d cry if I want to

Chip bellwether Samsung Electronics Co is expected to report its largest-ever quarterly profit on Thursday, but blowout numbers alone may not be enough to reassure investors that memory-chip demand is durable and high product prices can be locked in through long-term contracts.
